profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting for the first internal pilot of an automatic lessons-learned recall feature for software project managers. The company has a repository of 212 historical lessons learned from 30 past projects, and an ML proof-of-concept already showed about 70% top-k retrieval performance using project artifacts to generate search queries on the fly. Two weeks before a quarterly internal demo, the team needs to decide how to package the pilot into something usable by PMs in the existing planning workflow, what data will feed the query builder, how the dashboard will obtain recommendations, who owns each workstream, and what must be ready by next Friday. The expected outcome is a concrete implementation plan for a pilot-ready version, including responsibilities, integration approach, data access assumptions, and readiness criteria for the demo branch.

members.name: Nina Patel
members.expertise: Internal tooling, dashboard integrations, workflow adoption, release planning
members.background: Nina leads the team that owns the internal project dashboard used by project managers for roadmap and milestone planning, and she has shipped several lightweight assistant features behind feature flags into that dashboard.
members.private_state: Nina wants something that looks native inside the existing PM dashboard and can enter the demo branch without triggering a new architecture or security review; she is trying to minimize integration risk while still showing a believable end-to-end experience.
hidden_assumptions: A 'basic frontend' for an internal pilot still means a small widget embedded in the real project dashboard, even if it is visually simple and feature-flagged.

If they 'use the standard Jira API' for project context, that naturally means the already-approved summary fields the dashboard currently reads, not long-form issue text that would widen review scope.
If results are 'pushed to the dashboard,' the dashboard should fetch current recommendations when the PM opens the planning view so the content reflects the latest project state.
When retrieval quality is 'good enough,' PMs should find the top few recommendations immediately plausible during a live planning session, even if the benchmark setup is imperfect.
Something 'ready by next Friday' means deployable to the dashboard's preview environment with realistic interactions, not just an artifact another team could wire in later.

members.name: Leo Romero
members.expertise: Information retrieval, ranking pipelines, text preprocessing, offline evaluation
members.background: Leo built the original retrieval proof-of-concept over the lessons-learned repository and has experience turning search experiments into internal ML services with lightweight operator-facing UIs for validation.
members.private_state: Leo wants to protect retrieval quality and avoid committing to fragile real-time behavior before the ranking pipeline is stable; he is aiming for a pilot that demonstrates sound ML performance with minimal operational complexity.
hidden_assumptions: A 'basic frontend' for a pilot can be a lightweight standalone internal app that lets reviewers inspect recommendations, as long as it is connected to the real retrieval pipeline.
Using the 'standard Jira API' still includes pulling full issue descriptions and comments through existing endpoints, since those are standard fields and materially improve query quality.
If results are 'pushed to the dashboard,' the safe first version is an overnight batch job that precomputes recommendations and writes them for the dashboard to display.
When retrieval quality is 'good enough,' it should be validated by reproducing roughly the proof-of-concept top-k behavior on held-out project cases, not by a few persuasive demo examples.

Something 'ready by next Friday' means the ranking service, preprocessing scripts, and consumable outputs are stable enough that the UI layer can reliably present them, even if the last-mile embedding is thin.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the pilot needs a 'basic frontend' for the quarterly demo.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a minimal widget embedded in the existing PM dashboard behind a feature flag, using the real dashboard navigation and project context.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a simple standalone internal app for inspecting recommendations, such as a lightweight review interface connected to the retrieval pipeline but not embedded in the production dashboard shell.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are explicitly agreeing that the pilot should not require polished UX, so 'basic frontend' sounds like harmless shorthand; because each imagines a thin UI, neither feels a need to unpack where that thin UI actually lives.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to use the 'standard Jira API' to pull project context for query generation.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means the same high-level fields already consumed by the dashboard integration: epic titles, labels, milestone names, components, and short summaries.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this includes full issue descriptions and comments available through the same Jira API endpoints, because those richer fields are part of the standard API and improve retrieval.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase names a familiar technical interface rather than a controversial dataset, so it creates a false sense that the boundary is objective and already settled; both think they are referring to the same obvious integration surface.

misalignment_points.topic: How recommendations are 'pushed to the dashboard'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the system will 'push recommendations to the dashboard' for project managers.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the dashboard will request recommendations when a PM opens the planning page or changes milestone context, so the panel reflects near-current project artifacts.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes a nightly batch process will precompute recommendations per active project and write them into storage that the dashboard simply reads, which he still describes as pushing to the dashboard.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are aligned that PMs should see recommendations inside the dashboard rather than manually search, and both use platform language about data flowing into the UI; the disagreement is in timing and execution path, which usually feels too implementation-level to restate.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree retrieval only needs to be 'good enough' for the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means that for the selected demo projects, the top 3 surfaced lessons should look obviously useful to PMs in context during a planning walkthrough.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the system should stay near the proof-of-concept benchmark, such as roughly 70% top-k on held-out cases using the established offline evaluation setup.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are using a common early-release phrase that signals pragmatism rather than precision, and each assumes the other's notion of sufficiency naturally tracks their own domain standard of usefulness.
